overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of two early challenges to atomistic accounts of perception. You'll be asked about the constancy hypothesis, figure–ground, the grouping principles, Goldstein's holism, and the concrete/abstract distinction in the Schneider case.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

options.html: That perceived objects keep a constant size as we move
options.text: That perceived objects keep a constant size as we move
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That describes perceptual constancy, a different idea. The constancy hypothesis assumes each local stimulus yields a fixed sensation.

options.html: That each local stimulus yields a fixed sensation in any context
options.text: That each local stimulus yields a fixed sensation in any context
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Köhler named and criticized this assumption, on which elementism relied.

options.html: That perception stays constant across different observers
options.text: That perception stays constant across different observers
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The constancy hypothesis concerns stimulus and sensation: each local stimulus yields a fixed sensation, whatever its context.

options.html: That the organism keeps a constant balance with its milieu
options.text: That the organism keeps a constant balance with its milieu
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's closer to Goldstein's idea of equilibrium. The constancy hypothesis assumes each local stimulus yields a fixed sensation.

forms.stemHtml: In Rubin's vase–faces drawing, the image reverses from a vase to two faces. What changes during the reversal?

options.html: The pattern of light reaching the eyes
options.text: The pattern of light reaching the eyes
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nothing in the stimulus changes. What changes is which region is organized as figure and which as ground.

options.html: Which region is figure and which is ground
options.text: Which region is figure and which is ground
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The contour belongs to one side at a time, and the reversal happens without any change in the stimulus.

options.html: The number of separate sensations received
options.text: The number of separate sensations received
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The stimulus stays the same. What changes is the figure–ground organization.

options.html: The colors of the vase and the two faces
options.text: The colors of the vase and the two faces
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The colors don't change. What changes is which region is organized as figure and which as ground.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are among Wertheimer's grouping principles? (Select all that apply.)

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Elements close together are seen as belonging together.
Correct! Elements alike in color, shape, or size are seen as belonging together.
Correct! Elements that continue a smooth line or curve are seen as belonging together.
Sorry, that's incorrect. Association is how elementism combines sensations, which the Gestalt psychologists rejected.
Sorry, that's incorrect. The constancy hypothesis is the elementist assumption the Gestalt psychologists criticized.

forms.stemHtml: Faced with a task he can't meet, a brain-injured patient becomes agitated and disorganized, and can't do even things he could otherwise manage. What is Goldstein's term for this response? Enter two words.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Goldstein took the catastrophic reaction as evidence that the organism responds as a whole.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Goldstein calls this response a catastrophic reaction.

forms.stemHtml: Gelb and Goldstein reported that Schneider could scratch an itch on his nose but couldn't point to his nose on command. How did they interpret this?

options.html: As damage to the muscles of his arm
options.text: As damage to the muscles of his arm
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The concrete movement shows the arm works. They interpreted the pattern as a loss of the abstract attitude.

options.html: As a loss of the sense of touch in his face
options.text: As a loss of the sense of touch in his face
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Scratching the itch shows touch is intact. They interpreted the pattern as a loss of the abstract attitude.

options.html: As a simple defect in his visual system
options.text: As a simple defect in his visual system
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Vision alone can't explain why scratching succeeds and pointing fails. They interpreted the pattern as a loss of the abstract attitude.

options.html: As a loss of the abstract attitude
options.text: As a loss of the abstract attitude
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! They read the pattern as the loss of a whole capacity. Later scholarship has questioned the case's reliability.

title: Gestalt and the Organism
